motivation: Miyasaka first showed in 2009 that metal halide perovskites can act as photovoltaic absorbers. In 2012 Park demonstrated the first stable solid-state perovskite cells, and Snaith showed that the perovskite itself carries charge over long distances and works in planar thin-film devices. Together this work uncovered an unexpected class of semiconductors. They are solution-processed and full of defects, yet they have sharp absorption edges, long carrier diffusion lengths, low non-radiative losses and mixed ionic-electronic conduction. That combination changed how we think about defect tolerance in disordered semiconductors. Within a decade, single-junction efficiencies went from 3% to over 26%, and perovskite-silicon tandems now pass 34%, beyond the silicon limit. Perovskites are entering commercial production and offer a realistic route to cheaper, lower-carbon solar electricity at terawatt scale. This is fundamental semiconductor physics with direct consequences for climate mitigation.
